title: How Texas State University Punished a Student for Protesting White Supremacy
author: Yarden Azoulay Katz
content:
[![](https://www.counterpunch.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/word-
image-422626-1-680x885.jpeg)](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/08/16/how-
texas-state-university-punished-a-student-for-protesting-white-supremacy/)

Last fall, on September 16, 2025, Devion Canty was forced to withdraw from
Texas State University, just two weeks into his first semester in college.
Canty had attended a protest at a campus “memorial” for [Charlie
Kirk](https://racism.org/articles/defining-racism/white-
privilege/12835-charlie-kirk-white-supremacist), head of the white supremacist
group Turning Point USA, who had been assassinated days earlier (Kirk was shot
in the neck by a sniper while giving a public talk). Someone caught Canty on
video falling to the ground as if shot in the neck, in a theatrical imitation
of Kirk’s assassination. Texas Governor Greg Abbott shared the video on social
media in the late morning of that day,
[urging](https://x.com/GregAbbott_TX/status/1967986189136519573) Texas State
University to “expel the individual immediately.”

Within hours, Texas State University coerced Canty into withdrawing. As a
result, he lost his federal grants. He also had to abruptly leave his life at
Texas State behind – all while facing death threats and relentless racist
harassment. Determined to continue his education, Canty will be restarting
college this fall at Johnson C. Smith University, a historically Black college
in North Carolina, and is currently[
fundraising](https://www.givesendgo.com/help-devion-continue-his-education) to
pay the costs of housing.

Canty’s case shows yet again how universities cave under political pressure
from right-wing forces. But it also demonstrates how universities increasingly
deny access to anyone but the wealthy. That happens through increased tuition,
gentrification and unaffordable housing, and rules that make it harder to get
loans and later get out of student debt. This denial is a tool of political
control – a way to prevent radical struggles from forming on campus. In a time
of engineered scarcity, mutual aid is crucial to supporting those abused by
this system.

**Forced Out for Protesting White Supremacy**

Universities have a reputation for being slow, but under pressure from fascist
politicians they can be quite efficient. As the _University Star_
[reported](https://universitystar.com/33017/news/student-withdraws-from-
university-after-governor-shares-video-from-kirk-memorial/), Texas Governor
Abbott posted the video on social media at 11:17 am, on September 16, 2025,
calling to expel the Texas State University (TXST) student. By 12:30 pm, TXST
President Kelly Damphousse – a former prison guard whose academic
[research](https://www.icpsr.umich.edu/web/NACJD/studies/4639) area is
counterinsurgency – issued a statement saying the University is working on
identifying the student in the video. At 5:12 pm, he announced that “the
individual [Canty] is no longer a student at TXST.” In a university-wide email
sent out that day, Damphousse condemned Canty’s behavior, and even claimed
that the notion that many students might share Canty’s views of Kirk “cause[s]
some of our students to feel unsafe.”

It was Canty, meanwhile, who was getting barraged with racist insults and
death threats. At the campus protest that day, Canty and other Black students
were getting called n-word by those attending the Kirk “memorial,” while white
student protesters were called n-word lovers. Canty was spat at, and several
of the protesters were also pushed to the ground. Later, his cell phone number
got leaked and he began receiving death threats and racist messages from
strangers, forcing him to change his number. While his belongings were left
unceremoniously behind in his dorm room, his family pooled together their
money for a plane ticket back home and out of the danger closing in on him in
Texas.

TXST weaponized the fact that Canty was in real danger to get him to withdraw.
Once he was identified from the video on September 16, Canty received a phone
call from TXST’s Dean of Students. He was told he must pack his things
immediately and meet with her. A Black SUV, of the kind typically driven by
undercover police, picked him up from his dorm and took him to the University
police station. At the station, in a room with police officers present, Canty
was told by the Dean of Students that he should withdraw if he doesn’t want to
get expelled. Expulsion, the Dean of Students explained, would prevent him
from being admitted to other universities in the Texas public system (such as
Texas A&M).

Under these coercive conditions – and determined to continue his education
elsewhere – Canty had little choice but to withdraw.

As a result of TXST’s coercive maneuver, Canty lost all his federal grants and
financial aid. According to federal rules, a student must be enrolled long
enough for the grants to get activated; the early withdrawal had put him in
violation of these rules. As the [fundraiser](https://www.givesendgo.com/help-
devion-continue-his-education) for Canty puts it, “Given this country’s long
history of denying Black youth their right to learn, it is difficult not to
view the university administration’s actions within that same racist context.”

Texas State’s draconian handling of Canty fits with the University’s wider
pattern of repression. TXST has recently terminated three of its faculty
members over their political speech: [Idris Robinson](https://defend-idris-
robinson.org/), [Tom Alter](https://defendtomalter.org/), and [Saeed
Moshfegh](https://universitystar.com/35519/news/professor-considers-lawsuit-
against-texas-state-alleges-censorship/). Robinson, a tenure-track philosophy
professor, was terminated for expressing solidarity with the Palestinian
liberation struggle in an off-campus talk, after Zionist agitators began[
smearing him](https://www.counterpunch.org/2026/04/22/their-chaos-is-our-
peace-fighting-zionist-repression-in-texas-and-beyond/) on social media.
Robinson sued TXST, and in May 2026 a federal judge in Texas
[ordered](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/may/14/texas-professor-
fired-palestine-idris-robinson) the University to reinstate him, with pay, for
a year or until the trial resolves (the case is ongoing). Alter, who was a
tenured history professor, was similarly
[fired](https://www.insidehighered.com/news/faculty/academic-
freedom/2026/05/07/how-firing-turned-fight-academic-freedom) for an off-campus
speech after a fascist influencer made a video smearing him. Alter also sued
TXST and was reinstated by a court order only to be fired a second time; his
case is also ongoing. Moshfegh, an Iranian physics lecturer, put up a sign
declaring his office “a safe space for immigrants.” He was reprimanded, and
later TXST [decided](https://universitystar.com/35519/news/professor-
considers-lawsuit-against-texas-state-alleges-censorship/) not to renew his
contract.

In the cases of Robinson and Alter, just as in Canty’s case, TXST quickly met
the demands of external right-wing forces.

**Universities… but Only for the Rich**

The instances of faculty repression at TXST are important and deserve the
attention they have received, but Canty’s case has mostly disappeared from
view. As an undergraduate student, Canty is in a highly precarious position.
His total yearly housing costs at Johnson C. Smith, where he will start this
fall, are around $16,000 (and he currently needs to raise at least $8,000 by
August 26, 2026). And like many students who don’t come from families with
wealth, Canty doesn’t have someone who can co-sign a loan for him.

Canty’s fight to continue his education is taking place as college is becoming
increasingly unaffordable. Tuition rates have skyrocketed, along with student
debt. Today, about 42.6 million people are indebted through federal student
loans, totaling [$1.7 trillion](https://fsapartners.ed.gov/knowledge-
center/library/electronic-announcements/2026-06-23/federal-student-aid-posts-
updated-reports-fsa-data-center). In July 2026, the Trump administration made
these loans more restrictive: under the [new
rules](https://www.cnn.com/2026/07/01/business/trump-student-loans), even
those in the lowest income brackets will have to start paying their loans
sooner, with larger monthly payments. The new rules also place restrictions on
loans to parents paying for their children’s college. Unfortunately, over the
last decades major universities have been investing in anything but making
themselves more accessible. They have [taken
over](https://www.hachettebookgroup.com/titles/davarian-l-baldwin/in-the-
shadow-of-the-ivory-tower/9781568588926/?lens=bold-type-books) whole cities,
drawing corporate partnerships and luxury real estate developers, fueling
gentrification, and causing rent and food prices to go up.

Source: National Center for Education Statistics (NCES).

With the higher costs of everything, who can afford college, even at a
“public” institution? At the University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, where I work,
[12% of
undergraduates](https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2023/09/11/upshot/college-
income-lookup.html) have parents who are in the top 1% (based only on income,
excluding other assets). In theory, it’s a “public” university. In practice,
it’s a private wealth generating machine that caters to wealthy students,
donors, corporations, and real estate developers. The same applies to most
major US universities, whether public or private.

TXST is somewhat different in that [less than
2%](https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/projects/college-mobility/texas-state-
university) of its undergraduates come from the top 1%. It’s a university that
serves the broad public, at least on paper. Yet Canty’s story shows how the
mechanisms used to discipline students still disproportionately punish
working-class and poor students. One “misstep,” and you could lose everything.
How sickening it is that the Governor of Texas, a university president who
makes close to [$1
million](https://texascollegesalaries.com/institution/texas-state-
university/department/presidents-office/employee/kelly-r-damphousse), and
their teams of obedient middle-class professionals used their resources to try
to ruin the life of an 18-year-old college student, simply because he moved
his body in public space in a way they disapprove of.

It is as necessary as ever to support those harmed by this system.
